3PARA RAT has a command to retrieve metadata for files on disk as well as a command to list the current working directory. http://cdn0.vox-cdn.com/assets/4589853/crowdstrike-intelligence-report-putter-panda.original.pdf
3PARA RAT has a command to set certain attributes such as creation/modification timestamps on files. http://cdn0.vox-cdn.com/assets/4589853/crowdstrike-intelligence-report-putter-panda.original.pdf

Use: ADVSTORESHELL connects to port 80 of a C2 server using Wininet API. Data is exchanged via HTTP POSTs. https://securelist.com/sofacy-apt-hits-high-profile-targets-with-updated-toolset/72924/
ADVSTORESHELL encrypts with the 3DES algorithm and a hardcoded key prior to exfiltration. http://www.welivesecurity.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/10/eset-sednit-part-2.pdf

ADVSTORESHELL compresses output data generated by command execution with a custom implementation of the Lempel–Ziv–Welch (LZW) algorithm. http://www.welivesecurity.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/10/eset-sednit-part-2.pdf

ADVSTORESHELL achieves persistence by adding itself to the HKCU\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run Registry key.   https://securelist.com/sofacy-apt-hits-high-profile-targets-with-updated-toolset/72924/
ADVSTORESHELL can create a remote shell and run a given command.  http://www.welivesecurity.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/10/eset-sednit-part-2.pdf
C2 traffic from ADVSTORESHELL is encrypted, then encoded with Base64 encoding. https://securelist.com/sofacy-apt-hits-high-profile-targets-with-updated-toolset/72924/
ADVSTORESHELL stores output from command execution in a .dat file in the %TEMP% directory. http://www.welivesecurity.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/10/eset-sednit-part-2.pdf

A variant of ADVSTORESHELL encrypts some C2 with 3DES. https://download.bitdefender.com/resources/media/materials/white-papers/en/Bitdefender_In-depth_analysis_of_APT28%E2%80%93The_Political_Cyber-Espionage.pdf

A variant of ADVSTORESHELL encrypts some C2 with RSA. https://download.bitdefender.com/resources/media/materials/white-papers/en/Bitdefender_In-depth_analysis_of_APT28%E2%80%93The_Political_Cyber-Espionage.pdf

Some variants of ADVSTORESHELL achieve persistence by registering the payload as a Shell Icon Overlay handler COM object. http://www.welivesecurity.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/10/eset-sednit-part-2.pdf
ADVSTORESHELL exfiltrates data over the same channel used for C2. http://www.welivesecurity.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/10/eset-sednit-part-2.pdf
ADVSTORESHELL can list files and directories.  http://www.welivesecurity.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/10/eset-sednit-part-2.pdf
ADVSTORESHELL can delete files and directories. http://www.welivesecurity.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/10/eset-sednit-part-2.pdf
ADVSTORESHELL can perform keylogging.  http://www.welivesecurity.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/10/eset-sednit-part-2.pdf

ADVSTORESHELL is capable of setting and deleting Registry values. https://download.bitdefender.com/resources/media/materials/white-papers/en/Bitdefender_In-depth_analysis_of_APT28%E2%80%93The_Political_Cyber-Espionage.pdf

ADVSTORESHELL is capable of starting a process using CreateProcess. https://download.bitdefender.com/resources/media/materials/white-papers/en/Bitdefender_In-depth_analysis_of_APT28%E2%80%93The_Political_Cyber-Espionage.pdf

Most of the strings in ADVSTORESHELL are encrypted with an XOR-based algorithm; some strings are also encrypted with 3DES and reversed. API function names are also reversed, presumably to avoid detection in memory.  https://securelist.com/sofacy-apt-hits-high-profile-targets-with-updated-toolset/72924/
ADVSTORESHELL can list connected devices. http://www.welivesecurity.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/10/eset-sednit-part-2.pdf
ADVSTORESHELL can list running processes. http://www.welivesecurity.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/10/eset-sednit-part-2.pdf
ADVSTORESHELL can enumerate registry keys.  http://www.welivesecurity.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/10/eset-sednit-part-2.pdf
ADVSTORESHELL collects, compresses, encrypts, and exfiltrates data to the C2 server every 10 minutes. http://www.welivesecurity.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/10/eset-sednit-part-2.pdf

ADVSTORESHELL has used rundll32.exe in a Registry value to establish persistence. https://download.bitdefender.com/resources/media/materials/white-papers/en/Bitdefender_In-depth_analysis_of_APT28%E2%80%93The_Political_Cyber-Espionage.pdf
ADVSTORESHELL can run Systeminfo to gather information about the victim.  http://www.welivesecurity.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/10/eset-sednit-part-2.pdf

Cardinal RAT establishes Persistence by setting the HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Windows\Load Registry key to point to its executable. https://researchcenter.paloaltonetworks.com/2017/04/unit42-cardinal-rat-active-two-years/

Cardinal RAT uses a secret key with a series of XOR and addition operations to encrypt C2 traffic. https://researchcenter.paloaltonetworks.com/2017/04/unit42-cardinal-rat-active-two-years/
Cardinal RAT can communicate over multiple C2 host and port combinations. https://researchcenter.paloaltonetworks.com/2017/04/unit42-cardinal-rat-active-two-years/

Cardinal RAT checks its current working directory upon execution and also contains watchdog functionality that ensures its executable is located in the correct path (else it will rewrite the payload). https://researchcenter.paloaltonetworks.com/2017/04/unit42-cardinal-rat-active-two-years/
Cardinal RAT can uninstall itself, including deleting its executable. https://researchcenter.paloaltonetworks.com/2017/04/unit42-cardinal-rat-active-two-years/
Cardinal RAT can download and execute additional payloads. https://researchcenter.paloaltonetworks.com/2017/04/unit42-cardinal-rat-active-two-years/

Cardinal RAT contains watchdog functionality that ensures its process is always running, else spawns a new instance. https://researchcenter.paloaltonetworks.com/2017/04/unit42-cardinal-rat-active-two-years/
Cardinal RAT injects into a newly spawned process created from a native Windows executable. https://researchcenter.paloaltonetworks.com/2017/04/unit42-cardinal-rat-active-two-years/
Cardinal RAT can act as a reverse proxy. https://researchcenter.paloaltonetworks.com/2017/04/unit42-cardinal-rat-active-two-years/

Cardinal RAT can capture screenshots. https://researchcenter.paloaltonetworks.com/2017/04/unit42-cardinal-rat-active-two-years/

Cardinal RAT can collect the hostname, Microsoft Windows version, and processor architecture from a victim machine. https://researchcenter.paloaltonetworks.com/2017/04/unit42-cardinal-rat-active-two-years/
Cardinal RAT can collect the username from a victim machine. https://researchcenter.paloaltonetworks.com/2017/04/unit42-cardinal-rat-active-two-years/
Cardinal RAT lures victims into executing malicious macros embedded within Microsoft Excel documents. https://researchcenter.paloaltonetworks.com/2017/04/unit42-cardinal-rat-active-two-years/

Use: Cobalt Strike can use a number of known techniques to bypass Windows UAC.  https://web.archive.org/web/20210825130434/https://cobaltstrike.com/downloads/csmanual38.pdf
Cobalt Strike can use sudo to run a command. https://web.archive.org/web/20210708035426/https://www.cobaltstrike.com/downloads/csmanual43.pdf
Cobalt Strike can steal access tokens from exiting processes.  https://web.archive.org/web/20210825130434/https://cobaltstrike.com/downloads/csmanual38.pdf
Cobalt Strike can make tokens from known credentials. https://web.archive.org/web/20210825130434/https://cobaltstrike.com/downloads/csmanual38.pdf
Cobalt Strike can spawn processes with alternate PPIDs.  https://blog.cobaltstrike.com/2017/05/23/cobalt-strike-3-8-whos-your-daddy/

Cobalt Strike can determine if the user on an infected machine is in the admin or domain admin group. https://www.cybereason.com/blog/dropping-anchor-from-a-trickbot-infection-to-the-discovery-of-the-anchor-malware

Cobalt Strike can conduct peer-to-peer communication over Windows named pipes encapsulated in the SMB protocol. All protocols use their standard assigned ports.  https://web.archive.org/web/20210825130434/https://cobaltstrike.com/downloads/csmanual38.pdf

Cobalt Strike can use a custom command and control protocol that can be encapsulated in HTTP or HTTPS. All protocols use their standard assigned ports.    https://web.archive.org/web/20210825130434/https://cobaltstrike.com/downloads/csmanual38.pdf

Cobalt Strike can use a custom command and control protocol that can be encapsulated in DNS. All protocols use their standard assigned ports.   https://web.archive.org/web/20210825130434/https://cobaltstrike.com/downloads/csmanual38.pdf
Cobalt Strike can download a hosted "beacon" payload using BITSAdmin.   https://www.cobaltstrike.com/help-scripted-web-delivery

Cobalt Strike can perform browser pivoting and inject into a user's browser to inherit cookies, authenticated HTTP sessions, and client SSL certificates.  https://web.archive.org/web/20210825130434/https://cobaltstrike.com/downloads/csmanual38.pdf

Cobalt Strike can execute a payload on a remote host with PowerShell. This technique does not write any data to disk.   Cobalt Strike can also use PowerSploit and other scripting frameworks to perform execution.    https://web.archive.org/web/20210825130434/https://cobaltstrike.com/downloads/csmanual38.pdf
Cobalt Strike uses a command-line interface to interact with systems.   https://www.cobaltstrike.com/downloads/reports/tacticstechniquesandprocedures.pdf
Cobalt Strike can use VBA to perform execution.   https://www.cobaltstrike.com/downloads/reports/tacticstechniquesandprocedures.pdf
Cobalt Strike can use Python to perform execution.    https://www.cobaltstrike.com/downloads/reports/tacticstechniquesandprocedures.pdf

The Cobalt Strike System Profiler can use JavaScript to perform reconnaissance actions. https://talos-intelligence-site.s3.amazonaws.com/production/document_files/files/000/095/031/original/Talos_Cobalt_Strike.pdf
Cobalt Strike can install a new service. https://www.cobaltstrike.com/downloads/reports/tacticstechniquesandprocedures.pdf
Cobalt Strike can use Base64, URL-safe Base64, or NetBIOS encoding in its C2 traffic. https://web.archive.org/web/20210708035426/https://www.cobaltstrike.com/downloads/csmanual43.pdf
Cobalt Strike can collect data from a local system.  https://www.cobaltstrike.com/downloads/reports/tacticstechniquesandprocedures.pdf

Cobalt Strike can mimic the HTTP protocol for C2 communication, while hiding the actual data in either an HTTP header, URI parameter, the transaction body, or appending it to the URI. https://web.archive.org/web/20210708035426/https://www.cobaltstrike.com/downloads/csmanual43.pdf
Cobalt Strike will break large data sets into smaller chunks for exfiltration. https://web.archive.org/web/20210825130434/https://cobaltstrike.com/downloads/csmanual38.pdf

Cobalt Strike can deobfuscate shellcode using a rolling XOR and decrypt metadata from Beacon sessions.  https://talos-intelligence-site.s3.amazonaws.com/production/document_files/files/000/095/031/original/Talos_Cobalt_Strike.pdf

Cobalt Strike has the ability to use AES-256 symmetric encryption in CBC mode with HMAC-SHA-256 to encrypt task commands and XOR to encrypt shell code and configuration data. https://talos-intelligence-site.s3.amazonaws.com/production/document_files/files/000/095/031/original/Talos_Cobalt_Strike.pdf

Cobalt Strike can use RSA asymmetric encryption with PKCS1 padding to encrypt data sent to the C2 server. https://talos-intelligence-site.s3.amazonaws.com/production/document_files/files/000/095/031/original/Talos_Cobalt_Strike.pdf

Cobalt Strike can exploit Oracle Java vulnerabilities for execution, including CVE-2011-3544, CVE-2013-2465, CVE-2012-4681, and CVE-2013-2460.  https://talos-intelligence-site.s3.amazonaws.com/production/document_files/files/000/095/031/original/Talos_Cobalt_Strike.pdf
Cobalt Strike can exploit vulnerabilities such as MS14-058.  https://www.cobaltstrike.com/downloads/reports/tacticstechniquesandprocedures.pdf
Cobalt Strike can explore files on a compromised system. https://web.archive.org/web/20210708035426/https://www.cobaltstrike.com/downloads/csmanual43.pdf
Cobalt Strike can use spoof arguments in spawned processes that execute beacon commands. https://web.archive.org/web/20210708035426/https://www.cobaltstrike.com/downloads/csmanual43.pdf

Cobalt Strike has the ability to use Smart Applet attacks to disable the Java SecurityManager sandbox.  https://talos-intelligence-site.s3.amazonaws.com/production/document_files/files/000/095/031/original/Talos_Cobalt_Strike.pdf
Cobalt Strike can timestomp any files or payloads placed on a target machine to help them blend in.  https://web.archive.org/web/20210825130434/https://cobaltstrike.com/downloads/csmanual38.pdf
Cobalt Strike can deliver additional payloads to victim machines.  https://talos-intelligence-site.s3.amazonaws.com/production/document_files/files/000/095/031/original/Talos_Cobalt_Strike.pdf
Cobalt Strike can track key presses with a keylogger module.   https://web.archive.org/web/20210825130434/https://cobaltstrike.com/downloads/csmanual38.pdf

Cobalt Strike can modify Registry values within HKEY_CURRENT_USER\Software\Microsoft\Office\\Excel\Security\AccessVBOM\ to enable the execution of additional code. https://talos-intelligence-site.s3.amazonaws.com/production/document_files/files/000/095/031/original/Talos_Cobalt_Strike.pdf

Cobalt Strike's Beacon payload is capable of running shell commands without cmd.exe and PowerShell commands without powershell.exe   https://web.archive.org/web/20210825130434/https://cobaltstrike.com/downloads/csmanual38.pdf
Cobalt Strike can perform port scans from an infected host.   https://web.archive.org/web/20210825130434/https://cobaltstrike.com/downloads/csmanual38.pdf
Cobalt Strike can query shared drives on the local system. https://www.cobaltstrike.com/downloads/reports/tacticstechniquesandprocedures.pdf

Cobalt Strike can be configured to use TCP, ICMP, and UDP for C2 communications.  https://talos-intelligence-site.s3.amazonaws.com/production/document_files/files/000/095/031/original/Talos_Cobalt_Strike.pdf

Cobalt Strike can hash functions to obfuscate calls to the Windows API and use a public/private key pair to encrypt Beacon session metadata.  https://talos-intelligence-site.s3.amazonaws.com/production/document_files/files/000/095/031/original/Talos_Cobalt_Strike.pdf

Cobalt Strike includes a capability to modify the Beacon payload to eliminate known signatures or unpacking methods.  https://web.archive.org/web/20210825130434/https://cobaltstrike.com/downloads/csmanual38.pdf

Cobalt Strike has the ability to use an Excel Workbook to execute additional code by enabling Office to trust macros and execute code without user permission. https://talos-intelligence-site.s3.amazonaws.com/production/document_files/files/000/095/031/original/Talos_Cobalt_Strike.pdf
Cobalt Strike can spawn a job to inject into LSASS memory and dump password hashes. https://web.archive.org/web/20210708035426/https://www.cobaltstrike.com/downloads/csmanual43.pdf
Cobalt Strike can recover hashed passwords. https://web.archive.org/web/20210825130434/https://cobaltstrike.com/downloads/csmanual38.pdf
Cobalt Strike can use net localgroup to list local groups on a system. https://web.archive.org/web/20210708035426/https://www.cobaltstrike.com/downloads/csmanual43.pdf
Cobalt Strike can identify targets by querying account groups on a domain contoller. https://web.archive.org/web/20210708035426/https://www.cobaltstrike.com/downloads/csmanual43.pdf
Cobalt Strike's Beacon payload can collect information on process details.   https://web.archive.org/web/20210825130434/https://cobaltstrike.com/downloads/csmanual38.pdf

Industroyer can enumerate remote computers in the compromised network. https://www.welivesecurity.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/06/Win32_Industroyer.pdf

Industroyer’s 61850 payload component enumerates connected network adapters and their corresponding IP addresses. https://www.welivesecurity.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/06/Win32_Industroyer.pdf
Industroyer can use supplied user credentials to execute processes and stop services. https://www.welivesecurity.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/06/Win32_Industroyer.pdf

The Industroyer SPIROTEC DoS module places the victim device into firmware update mode. This is a legitimate use case under normal circumstances, but in this case is used the adversary to prevent the SPIROTEC from performing its designed protective functions. As a result the normal safeguards are disabled, leaving an unprotected link in the electric transmission.  https://dragos.com/wp-content/uploads/CRASHOVERRIDE.pdf
Industroyer automatically collects protocol object data to learn about control devices in the environment.  https://www.welivesecurity.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/06/Win32_Industroyer.pdf

In Industroyer the first COM port from the configuration file is used for the actual communication and the two other COM ports are just opened to prevent other processes accessing them. Thus, the IEC 101 payload component is able to take over and maintain control of the RTU device.  https://www.welivesecurity.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/06/Win32_Industroyer.pdf

Industroyer uses the first COM port from the configuration file for the communication and the other two COM ports are opened to prevent other processes accessing them. This may block processes or operators from getting reporting messages from a device.  https://www.welivesecurity.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/06/Win32_Industroyer.pdf

In Industroyer the first COM port from the configuration file is used for the actual communication and the two other COM ports are just opened to prevent other processes accessing them. Thus, the IEC 101 payload component is able to take over and maintain control of the RTU device.  https://www.welivesecurity.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/06/Win32_Industroyer.pdf

The Industroyer IEC 104 module has 3 modes available to perform its attack. These modes are range, shift, and sequence. The range mode operates in 2 stages. The first stage of range mode gathers Information Object Addresses (IOA) and sends select and execute packets to switch the state. The second stage of range mode has an infinite loop where it will switch the state of all of the previously discovered IOAs. Shift mode is similar to range mode, but instead of staying within the same range, it will add a shift value to the default range values.  https://www.welivesecurity.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/06/Win32_Industroyer.pdf

The name of the Industroyer payload DLL is supplied by the attackers via a command line parameter supplied in one of the main backdoors execute a shell command commands.  https://www.welivesecurity.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/06/Win32_Industroyer.pdf

Industroyer attempts to connect with a hardcoded internal proxy on TCP 3128 [default Squid proxy]. If established, the backdoor attempts to reach an external C2 server via the internal proxy.  https://dragos.com/blog/crashoverride/CrashOverride-01.pdf

Industroyer has a destructive wiper that overwrites all ICS configuration files across the hard drives and all mapped network drives specifically targeting ABB PCM600 configuration files.  https://dragos.com/blog/crashoverride/CrashOverride-01.pdf
Industroyer is able to block serial COM channels temporarily causing a denial of control.  https://www.welivesecurity.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/06/Win32_Industroyer.pdf

The Industroyer SIPROTEC DoS module exploits the CVE-2015-5374 vulnerability in order to render a Siemens SIPROTEC device unresponsive. Once this vulnerability is successfully exploited, the target device stops responding to any commands until it is rebooted manually.   Once the tool is executed it sends specifically crafted packets to port 50,000 of the target IP addresses using UDP. The UDP packet contains the following 18 byte payload: 0x11 49 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 28 9E.  https://www.welivesecurity.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/06/Win32_Industroyer.pdf
Industroyer is able to block serial COM channels temporarily causing a denial of view.  https://www.welivesecurity.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/06/Win32_Industroyer.pdf

The Industroyer SIPROTEC DoS module exploits the CVE-2015-5374 vulnerability in order to render a Siemens SIPROTEC device unresponsive. While the vulnerability does not directly cause the restart or shutdown of the device, the device must be restarted manually before it can resume operations.  https://www.welivesecurity.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/06/Win32_Industroyer.pdf

Industroyer's data wiper component removes the registry image path throughout the system and overwrites all files, rendering the system unusable.  https://www.welivesecurity.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/06/Win32_Industroyer.pdf

Industroyer contained a module which leveraged a vulnerability in the Siemens SIPROTEC relays (CVE-2015-5374) to create a Denial of Service against automated protective relays.  https://dragos.com/wp-content/uploads/CRASHOVERRIDE2018.pdf

Industroyer's data wiper component removes the registry image path throughout the system and overwrites all files, rendering the system unusable.  https://www.welivesecurity.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/06/Win32_Industroyer.pdf
Industroyer toggles breakers to the open state utilizing unauthorized command messages.  https://www.welivesecurity.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/06/Win32_Industroyer.pdf

Industroyer's OPC module can brute force values and will send out a 0x01 status which for the target systems equates to a Primary Variable Out of Limits misdirecting operators from understanding protective relay status.  https://www.welivesecurity.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/06/Win32_Industroyer.pdf

Industroyer's OPC and IEC 61850 protocol modules include the ability to send stVal requests to read the status of operational variables.  https://www.welivesecurity.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/06/Win32_Industroyer.pdf

Industroyer contains an IEC 61850 module that enumerates all connected network adapters to determine their TCP/IP subnet masks.  https://www.welivesecurity.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/06/Win32_Industroyer.pdf

The Industroyer IEC 61850 payload component has the ability to discover relevant devices in the infected host's network subnet by attempting to connect on port 102. 
Industroyer contains an OPC DA module that enumerates all OPC servers using the ICatInformation::EnumClassesOfCategories method with CATID_OPCDAServer20 category identifier and IOPCServer::GetStatus to identify the ones running.https://www.welivesecurity.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/06/Win32_Industroyer.pdf

The Industroyer IEC 61850 componentsends the domain-specific MMSgetNameListrequest to determine what logical nodes the device supports. It then searches the logical nodes for the CSW value, which indicates the device performs a circuit breaker or switch control function. 
Industroyer's OPC DA module also uses IOPCBrowseServerAddressSpace to look for items with the following strings: ctlSelOn, ctlOperOn, ctlSelOff, ctlOperOff, Pos and stVal. 
Industroyer IEC 60870-5-104 module includes a range mode to discover Information Object Addresses (IOAs) by enumerating through each. https://www.welivesecurity.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/06/Win32_Industroyer.pdf
Industroyer has the capability to stop a service itself, or to login as a user and stop a service as that user.  https://www.welivesecurity.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/06/Win32_Industroyer.pdf
Using its protocol payloads, Industroyer sends unauthorized commands to RTUs to change the state of equipment.  https://www.welivesecurity.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/06/Win32_Industroyer.pdf

MacMa can execute supplied shell commands and uses bash scripts to perform additional actions.  https://www.welivesecurity.com/2022/01/25/watering-hole-deploys-new-macos-malware-dazzlespy-asia/

MacMa installs a com.apple.softwareupdate.plist file in the /LaunchAgents folder with the RunAtLoad value set to true. Upon user login, MacMa is executed from /var/root/.local/softwareupdate with root privileges. Some variations also include the LimitLoadToSessionType key with the value Aqua, ensuring the MacMa only runs when there is a logged in GUI user.  https://www.welivesecurity.com/2022/01/25/watering-hole-deploys-new-macos-malware-dazzlespy-asia/

MacMa has stored collected files locally before exfiltration. https://objective-see.org/blog/blog_0x69.html
MacMa decrypts a downloaded file using AES-128-EBC with a custom delta. https://www.welivesecurity.com/2022/01/25/watering-hole-deploys-new-macos-malware-dazzlespy-asia/
MacMa has used TLS encryption to initialize a custom protocol for C2 communications. https://www.welivesecurity.com/2022/01/25/watering-hole-deploys-new-macos-malware-dazzlespy-asia/
MacMa exfiltrates data from a supplied path over its C2 channel. https://www.welivesecurity.com/2022/01/25/watering-hole-deploys-new-macos-malware-dazzlespy-asia/

MacMa can search for a specific file on the compromised computer and can enumerate files in Desktop, Downloads, and Documents folders. https://www.welivesecurity.com/2022/01/25/watering-hole-deploys-new-macos-malware-dazzlespy-asia/
MacMa can clear possible malware traces such as application logs. https://www.welivesecurity.com/2022/01/25/watering-hole-deploys-new-macos-malware-dazzlespy-asia/
MacMa can delete itself from the compromised computer. https://www.welivesecurity.com/2022/01/25/watering-hole-deploys-new-macos-malware-dazzlespy-asia/
MacMa has the capability to create and modify file timestamps. https://www.welivesecurity.com/2022/01/25/watering-hole-deploys-new-macos-malware-dazzlespy-asia/
MacMa has downloaded additional files, including an exploit for used privilege escalation.  https://www.welivesecurity.com/2022/01/25/watering-hole-deploys-new-macos-malware-dazzlespy-asia/

MacMa can use Core Graphics Event Taps to intercept user keystrokes from any text input field and saves them to text files. Text input fields include Spotlight, Finder, Safari, Mail, Messages, and other apps that have text fields for passwords.  https://objective-see.org/blog/blog_0x69.html
MacMa has used macOS API functions to perform tasks.  https://www.welivesecurity.com/2022/01/25/watering-hole-deploys-new-macos-malware-dazzlespy-asia/

MacMa has used TCP port 5633 for C2 Communication. https://www.welivesecurity.com/2022/01/25/watering-hole-deploys-new-macos-malware-dazzlespy-asia/
MacMa can enumerate running processes. https://www.welivesecurity.com/2022/01/25/watering-hole-deploys-new-macos-malware-dazzlespy-asia/
MacMa can manage remote screen sessions. https://www.welivesecurity.com/2022/01/25/watering-hole-deploys-new-macos-malware-dazzlespy-asia/

MacMa has used Apple’s Core Graphic APIs, such as CGWindowListCreateImageFromArray, to capture the user's screen and open windows.  https://www.welivesecurity.com/2022/01/25/watering-hole-deploys-new-macos-malware-dazzlespy-asia/
MacMa has removed the com.apple.quarantineattribute from the dropped file, $TMPDIR/airportpaird. https://www.welivesecurity.com/2022/01/25/watering-hole-deploys-new-macos-malware-dazzlespy-asia/

MacMa can collect information about a compromised computer, including: Hardware UUID, Mac serial number, macOS version, and disk sizes. https://www.welivesecurity.com/2022/01/25/watering-hole-deploys-new-macos-malware-dazzlespy-asia/
MacMa can collect IP addresses from a compromised host. https://www.welivesecurity.com/2022/01/25/watering-hole-deploys-new-macos-malware-dazzlespy-asia/
MacMa can collect the username from the compromised machine. https://www.welivesecurity.com/2022/01/25/watering-hole-deploys-new-macos-malware-dazzlespy-asia/

Use: Maze has communicated to hard-coded IP addresses via HTTP. https://www.mcafee.com/blogs/other-blogs/mcafee-labs/ransomware-maze/

Maze has created a file named "startup_vrun.bat" in the Startup folder of a virtual machine to establish persistence. https://news.sophos.com/en-us/2020/09/17/maze-attackers-adopt-ragnar-locker-virtual-machine-technique/

The Maze encryption process has used batch scripts with various commands.  https://www.fireeye.com/blog/threat-research/2020/05/tactics-techniques-procedures-associated-with-maze-ransomware-incidents.html

Maze has disrupted systems by encrypting files on targeted machines, claiming to decrypt files if a ransom payment is made. Maze has used the ChaCha algorithm, based on Salsa20, and an RSA algorithm to encrypt files. https://www.fireeye.com/blog/threat-research/2020/05/tactics-techniques-procedures-associated-with-maze-ransomware-incidents.html

Maze has forged POST strings with a random choice from a list of possibilities including "forum", "php", "view", etc. while making connection with the C2, hindering detection efforts. https://www.mcafee.com/blogs/other-blogs/mcafee-labs/ransomware-maze/

Maze operators have used VirtualBox and a Windows 7 virtual machine to run the ransomware; the virtual machine's configuration file mapped the shared network drives of the target company, presumably so Maze can encrypt files on the shared drives as well as the local machine. https://news.sophos.com/en-us/2020/09/17/maze-attackers-adopt-ragnar-locker-virtual-machine-technique/

Maze has disabled dynamic analysis and other security tools including IDA debugger, x32dbg, and OllyDbg.  It has also disabled Windows Defender's Real-Time Monitoring feature and attempted to disable endpoint protection services. https://www.mcafee.com/blogs/other-blogs/mcafee-labs/ransomware-maze/

Maze has used the "Wow64RevertWow64FsRedirection" function following attempts to delete the shadow volumes, in order to leave the system in the same state as it was prior to redirection. https://www.mcafee.com/blogs/other-blogs/mcafee-labs/ransomware-maze/
Maze has attempted to delete the shadow volumes of infected machines, once before and once after the encryption process.  https://www.mcafee.com/blogs/other-blogs/mcafee-labs/ransomware-maze/

Maze operators have created scheduled tasks masquerading as "Windows Update Security", "Windows Update Security Patches", and "Google Chrome Security Update" designed to launch the ransomware. https://news.sophos.com/en-us/2020/09/17/maze-attackers-adopt-ragnar-locker-virtual-machine-technique/

Maze has used several Windows API functions throughout the encryption process including IsDebuggerPresent, TerminateProcess, Process32FirstW, among others. https://www.mcafee.com/blogs/other-blogs/mcafee-labs/ransomware-maze/

Maze has decrypted strings and other important information during the encryption process. Maze also calls certain functions dynamically to hinder analysis. https://www.mcafee.com/blogs/other-blogs/mcafee-labs/ransomware-maze/

Maze has inserted large blocks of junk code, including some components to decrypt strings and other important information for later in the encryption process. https://www.mcafee.com/blogs/other-blogs/mcafee-labs/ransomware-maze/
Maze has gathered all of the running system processes. https://www.mcafee.com/blogs/other-blogs/mcafee-labs/ransomware-maze/
Maze has injected the malware DLL into a target process.  https://www.mcafee.com/blogs/other-blogs/mcafee-labs/ransomware-maze/

Maze has created scheduled tasks using name variants such as "Windows Update Security", "Windows Update Security Patches", and "Google Chrome Security Update", to launch Maze at a specific time. https://news.sophos.com/en-us/2020/09/17/maze-attackers-adopt-ragnar-locker-virtual-machine-technique/
Maze has stopped SQL services to ensure it can encrypt any database. https://news.sophos.com/en-us/2020/09/17/maze-attackers-adopt-ragnar-locker-virtual-machine-technique/

Maze has delivered components for its ransomware attacks using MSI files, some of which have been executed from the command-line using msiexec. https://news.sophos.com/en-us/2020/09/17/maze-attackers-adopt-ragnar-locker-virtual-machine-technique/
Maze has checked the language of the infected system using the "GetUSerDefaultUILanguage" function. https://www.mcafee.com/blogs/other-blogs/mcafee-labs/ransomware-maze/

Maze has checked the language of the machine with function GetUserDefaultUILanguage and terminated execution if the language matches with an entry in the predefined list. https://www.mcafee.com/blogs/other-blogs/mcafee-labs/ransomware-maze/

Maze has used the "WNetOpenEnumW", "WNetEnumResourceW", "WNetCloseEnum" and "WNetAddConnection2W" functions to enumerate the network resources on the infected machine. https://www.mcafee.com/blogs/other-blogs/mcafee-labs/ransomware-maze/

Maze has issued a shutdown command on a victim machine that, upon reboot, will run the ransomware within a VM. https://news.sophos.com/en-us/2020/09/17/maze-attackers-adopt-ragnar-locker-virtual-machine-technique/

Maze has used WMI to attempt to delete the shadow volumes on a machine, and to connect a virtual machine to the network domain of the victim organization's network.  https://www.mcafee.com/blogs/other-blogs/mcafee-labs/ransomware-maze/

Use: MESSAGETAP has XOR-encrypted and stored contents of SMS messages that matched its target list.  https://www.fireeye.com/blog/threat-research/2019/10/messagetap-who-is-reading-your-text-messages.html

MESSAGETAP checks two files, keyword_parm.txt and parm.txt, for instructions on how to target and save data parsed and extracted from SMS message data from the network traffic. If an SMS message contained either a phone number, IMSI number, or keyword that matched the predefined list, it is saved to a CSV file for later theft by the threat actor. https://www.fireeye.com/blog/threat-research/2019/10/messagetap-who-is-reading-your-text-messages.html

MESSAGETAP stored targeted SMS messages that matched its target list in CSV files on the compromised system. https://www.fireeye.com/blog/threat-research/2019/10/messagetap-who-is-reading-your-text-messages.html

After checking for the existence of two files, keyword_parm.txt and parm.txt, MESSAGETAP XOR decodes and read the contents of the files.  https://www.fireeye.com/blog/threat-research/2019/10/messagetap-who-is-reading-your-text-messages.html

MESSAGETAP checks for the existence of two configuration files (keyword_parm.txt and parm.txt) and attempts to read the files every 30 seconds. https://www.fireeye.com/blog/threat-research/2019/10/messagetap-who-is-reading-your-text-messages.html

Once loaded into memory, MESSAGETAP deletes the keyword_parm.txt and parm.txt configuration files from disk.  https://www.fireeye.com/blog/threat-research/2019/10/messagetap-who-is-reading-your-text-messages.html

MESSAGETAP uses the libpcap library to listen to all traffic and parses network protocols starting with Ethernet and IP layers. It continues parsing protocol layers including SCTP, SCCP, and TCAP and finally extracts SMS message data and routing metadata.  https://www.fireeye.com/blog/threat-research/2019/10/messagetap-who-is-reading-your-text-messages.html

After loading the keyword and phone data files, MESSAGETAP begins monitoring all network connections to and from the victim server.  https://www.fireeye.com/blog/threat-research/2019/10/messagetap-who-is-reading-your-text-messages.html

The worm then copies itself to the target and subsequently starts the target PLC again.  https://www.blackhat.com/docs/asia-16/materials/asia-16-Spenneberg-PLC-Blaster-A-Worm-Living-Solely-In-The-PLC-wp.pdf

The execution on the PLC can be stopped by violating the cycle time limit. The PLC-Blaster implements an endless loop triggering an error condition within the PLC with the impact of a DoS.  https://www.blackhat.com/docs/asia-16/materials/asia-16-Spenneberg-PLC-Blaster-A-Worm-Living-Solely-In-The-PLC-wp.pdf

PLC-Blaster may manipulate any outputs of the PLC. Using the POU POKE any value within the process image may be modified.  https://www.blackhat.com/docs/asia-16/materials/asia-16-Spenneberg-PLC-Blaster-A-Worm-Living-Solely-In-The-PLC-wp.pdf

PLC-Blaster's code is stored in OB9999. The original code on the target is untouched. The OB is automatically detected by the PLC and executed.  https://www.blackhat.com/docs/asia-16/materials/asia-16-Spenneberg-PLC-Blaster-A-Worm-Living-Solely-In-The-PLC-wp.pdf

PLC-Blaster copies itself to various Program Organization Units (POU) on the target device. The POUs include the Data Block, Function, and Function Block.  https://www.blackhat.com/docs/asia-16/materials/asia-16-Spenneberg-PLC-Blaster-A-Worm-Living-Solely-In-The-PLC-wp.pdf

PLC-Blaster uses the system function blocks TCON and TDISCON to initiate and destroy TCP connections to arbitrary systems. Buffers may be sent and received on these connections with TRCV und TSEND system function blocks.  https://www.blackhat.com/docs/asia-16/materials/asia-16-Spenneberg-PLC-Blaster-A-Worm-Living-Solely-In-The-PLC-wp.pdf

PLC-Blaster utilizes the PLC communication and management API to load executable Program Organization Units.  https://www.blackhat.com/docs/asia-16/materials/asia-16-Spenneberg-PLC-Blaster-A-Worm-Living-Solely-In-The-PLC-wp.pdf

PLC-Blaster scans the network to find other Siemens S7 PLC devices to infect. It locates these devices by checking for a service listening on TCP port 102.  https://www.blackhat.com/docs/asia-16/materials/asia-16-Spenneberg-PLC-Blaster-A-Worm-Living-Solely-In-The-PLC-wp.pdf

Use: Ryuk has attempted to adjust its token privileges to have the SeDebugPrivilege. https://www.crowdstrike.com/blog/big-game-hunting-with-ryuk-another-lucrative-targeted-ransomware/

Ryuk has used the Windows command line to create a Registry entry under HKEY_CURRENT_USER\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run to establish persistence. https://www.crowdstrike.com/blog/big-game-hunting-with-ryuk-another-lucrative-targeted-ransomware/
Ryuk has used cmd.exe to create a Registry entry to establish persistence. https://www.crowdstrike.com/blog/big-game-hunting-with-ryuk-another-lucrative-targeted-ransomware/

Ryuk has used a combination of symmetric (AES) and asymmetric (RSA) encryption to encrypt files. Files have been encrypted with their own AES key and given a file extension of .RYK. Encrypted directories have had a ransom note of RyukReadMe.txt written to the directory.  https://www.crowdstrike.com/blog/big-game-hunting-with-ryuk-another-lucrative-targeted-ransomware/
Ryuk has enumerated files and folders on all mounted drives. https://www.crowdstrike.com/blog/big-game-hunting-with-ryuk-another-lucrative-targeted-ransomware/
Ryuk can launch icacls /grant Everyone:F /T /C /Q to delete every access-based restrictions on files and directories. https://www.cert.ssi.gouv.fr/uploads/CERTFR-2021-CTI-006.pdf
Ryuk has stopped services related to anti-virus. https://www.fireeye.com/blog/threat-research/2019/01/a-nasty-trick-from-credential-theft-malware-to-business-disruption.html

Ryuk has used vssadmin Delete Shadows /all /quiet to to delete volume shadow copies and vssadmin resize shadowstorage to force deletion of shadow copies created by third-party applications. https://www.crowdstrike.com/blog/big-game-hunting-with-ryuk-another-lucrative-targeted-ransomware/
Ryuk can create .dll files that actually contain a Rich Text File format document. https://www.cert.ssi.gouv.fr/uploads/CERTFR-2021-CTI-006.pdf

Ryuk has constructed legitimate appearing installation folder paths by calling GetWindowsDirectoryW and then inserting a null byte at the fourth character of the path. For Windows Vista or higher, the path would appear as C:\Users\Public. https://www.crowdstrike.com/blog/big-game-hunting-with-ryuk-another-lucrative-targeted-ransomware/

Ryuk has used multiple native APIs including ShellExecuteW to run executables,GetWindowsDirectoryW to create folders, and VirtualAlloc, WriteProcessMemory, and CreateRemoteThread for process injection. https://www.crowdstrike.com/blog/big-game-hunting-with-ryuk-another-lucrative-targeted-ransomware/
Ryuk can use anti-disassembly and code transformation obfuscation techniques. https://www.crowdstrike.com/blog/wizard-spider-adversary-update/
Ryuk has called CreateToolhelp32Snapshot to enumerate all running processes. https://www.crowdstrike.com/blog/big-game-hunting-with-ryuk-another-lucrative-targeted-ransomware/

Ryuk has injected itself into remote processes to encrypt files using a combination of VirtualAlloc, WriteProcessMemory, and CreateRemoteThread. https://www.crowdstrike.com/blog/big-game-hunting-with-ryuk-another-lucrative-targeted-ransomware/
Ryuk has used the C$ network share for lateral movement. https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/ryuk-ransomware-uses-wake-on-lan-to-encrypt-offline-devices/
Ryuk can remotely create a scheduled task to execute itself on a system. https://www.cert.ssi.gouv.fr/uploads/CERTFR-2021-CTI-006.pdf
Ryuk has called kill.bat for stopping services, disabling services and killing processes. https://www.crowdstrike.com/blog/big-game-hunting-with-ryuk-another-lucrative-targeted-ransomware/

Ryuk has called GetLogicalDrives to emumerate all mounted drives, and GetDriveTypeW to determine the drive type. https://www.crowdstrike.com/blog/big-game-hunting-with-ryuk-another-lucrative-targeted-ransomware/

Ryuk has been observed to query the registry key HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Nls\Language and the value InstallLanguage. If the machine has the value 0x419 (Russian), 0x422 (Ukrainian), or 0x423 (Belarusian), it stops execution. https://www.crowdstrike.com/blog/big-game-hunting-with-ryuk-another-lucrative-targeted-ransomware/

Ryuk has called GetIpNetTable in attempt to identify all mounted drives and hosts that have Address Resolution Protocol (ARP) entries.  https://www.crowdstrike.com/blog/big-game-hunting-with-ryuk-another-lucrative-targeted-ransomware/
Ryuk has used Wake-on-Lan to power on turned off systems for lateral movement. https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/ryuk-ransomware-uses-wake-on-lan-to-encrypt-offline-devices/
Ryuk can use stolen domain admin accounts to move laterally within a victim domain. https://www.cert.ssi.gouv.fr/uploads/CERTFR-2021-CTI-006.pdf

An enterprise resource planning (ERP) manufacturing server was lost to the Ryuk attack. The manufacturing process had to rely on paper and existing orders to keep the shop floor open.  https://www.darkreading.com/attacks-breaches/how-a-manufacturing-firm-recovered-from-a-devastating-ransomware-attack/d/d-id/1334760

S-Type may create the file %HOMEPATH%\Start Menu\Programs\Startup\Realtek {Unique Identifier}.lnk, which points to the malicious msdtc.exe file already created in the %CommonFiles% directory. https://s7d2.scene7.com/is/content/cylance/prod/cylance-web/en-us/resources/knowledge-center/resource-library/reports/Op_Dust_Storm_Report.pdf

S-Type has provided the ability to execute shell commands on a compromised host. https://s7d2.scene7.com/is/content/cylance/prod/cylance-web/en-us/resources/knowledge-center/resource-library/reports/Op_Dust_Storm_Report.pdf

S-Type has uploaded data and files from a compromised host to its C2 servers. https://s7d2.scene7.com/is/content/cylance/prod/cylance-web/en-us/resources/knowledge-center/resource-library/reports/Op_Dust_Storm_Report.pdf

S-Type primarily uses port 80 for C2, but falls back to ports 443 or 8080 if initial communication fails. https://s7d2.scene7.com/is/content/cylance/prod/cylance-web/en-us/resources/knowledge-center/resource-library/reports/Op_Dust_Storm_Report.pdf
S-Type has deleted accounts it has created. https://s7d2.scene7.com/is/content/cylance/prod/cylance-web/en-us/resources/knowledge-center/resource-library/reports/Op_Dust_Storm_Report.pdf

S-Type has deleted files it has created on a compromised host. https://s7d2.scene7.com/is/content/cylance/prod/cylance-web/en-us/resources/knowledge-center/resource-library/reports/Op_Dust_Storm_Report.pdf

S-Type may save itself as a file named msdtc.exe, which is also the name of the legitimate Microsoft Distributed Transaction Coordinator service binary.  https://s7d2.scene7.com/is/content/cylance/prod/cylance-web/en-us/resources/knowledge-center/resource-library/reports/Op_Dust_Storm_Report.pdf

S-Type has used Windows APIs, including GetKeyboardType, NetUserAdd, and NetUserDel. https://s7d2.scene7.com/is/content/cylance/prod/cylance-web/en-us/resources/knowledge-center/resource-library/reports/Op_Dust_Storm_Report.pdf

The initial beacon packet for S-Type contains the operating system version and file system of the victim. https://s7d2.scene7.com/is/content/cylance/prod/cylance-web/en-us/resources/knowledge-center/resource-library/reports/Op_Dust_Storm_Report.pdf

Use: Stuxnet attempts to impersonate an anonymous token to enumerate bindings in the service control manager. https://www.wired.com/images_blogs/threatlevel/2010/11/w32_stuxnet_dossier.pdf
Stuxnet enumerates user accounts of the local host. https://www.wired.com/images_blogs/threatlevel/2010/11/w32_stuxnet_dossier.pdf
Stuxnet enumerates user accounts of the domain. https://www.wired.com/images_blogs/threatlevel/2010/11/w32_stuxnet_dossier.pdf
Stuxnet uses HTTP to communicate with a command and control server.  https://www.wired.com/images_blogs/threatlevel/2010/11/w32_stuxnet_dossier.pdf
Stuxnet encrypts exfiltrated data via C2 with static 31-byte long XOR keys. https://www.wired.com/images_blogs/threatlevel/2010/11/w32_stuxnet_dossier.pdf
Stuxnet uses a driver registered as a boot start service as the main load-point. https://www.wired.com/images_blogs/threatlevel/2010/11/w32_stuxnet_dossier.pdf
Stuxnet transforms encrypted binary data into an ASCII string in order to use it as a URL parameter value. https://www.wired.com/images_blogs/threatlevel/2010/11/w32_stuxnet_dossier.pdf
Stuxnet decrypts resources that are loaded into memory and executed. https://www.wired.com/images_blogs/threatlevel/2010/11/w32_stuxnet_dossier.pdf

Stuxnet encodes the payload of system information sent to the command and control servers using a one byte 0xFF XOR key. Stuxnet also uses a 31-byte long static byte string to XOR data sent to command and control servers. The servers use a different static key to encrypt replies to the implant. https://www.wired.com/images_blogs/threatlevel/2010/11/w32_stuxnet_dossier.pdf

Stuxnet checks for specific operating systems on 32-bit machines, Registry keys, and dates for vulnerabilities, and will exit execution if the values are not met. https://www.wired.com/images_blogs/threatlevel/2010/11/w32_stuxnet_dossier.pdf
Stuxnet sends compromised victim information via HTTP. https://www.wired.com/images_blogs/threatlevel/2010/11/w32_stuxnet_dossier.pdf
Stuxnet used MS10-073 and an undisclosed Task Scheduler vulnerability to escalate privileges on local Windows machines. https://www.wired.com/images_blogs/threatlevel/2010/11/w32_stuxnet_dossier.pdf
Stuxnet propagates using the MS10-061 Print Spooler and MS08-067 Windows Server Service vulnerabilities. https://www.wired.com/images_blogs/threatlevel/2010/11/w32_stuxnet_dossier.pdf
Stuxnet has the ability to generate new C2 domains. https://www.wired.com/images_blogs/threatlevel/2010/11/w32_stuxnet_dossier.pdf
Stuxnet uses a driver to scan for specific filesystem driver objects. https://www.wired.com/images_blogs/threatlevel/2010/11/w32_stuxnet_dossier.pdf
Stuxnet reduces the integrity level of objects to allow write actions. https://www.wired.com/images_blogs/threatlevel/2010/11/w32_stuxnet_dossier.pdf
Stuxnet can delete OLE Automation and SQL stored procedures used to store malicious payloads. https://www.wired.com/images_blogs/threatlevel/2010/11/w32_stuxnet_dossier.pdf

Stuxnet uses an RPC server that contains a routine for file deletion and also removes itself from the system through a DLL export by deleting specific files. https://www.wired.com/images_blogs/threatlevel/2010/11/w32_stuxnet_dossier.pdf
Stuxnet extracts and writes driver files that match the times of other legitimate files. https://www.wired.com/images_blogs/threatlevel/2010/11/w32_stuxnet_dossier.pdf

Stuxnet uses an RPC server that contains a file dropping routine and support for payload version updates for P2P communications within a victim network. https://www.wired.com/images_blogs/threatlevel/2010/11/w32_stuxnet_dossier.pdf
Stuxnet can create registry keys to load driver files. https://www.wired.com/images_blogs/threatlevel/2010/11/w32_stuxnet_dossier.pdf
Stuxnet uses the SetSecurityDescriptorDacl API to reduce object integrity levels. https://www.wired.com/images_blogs/threatlevel/2010/11/w32_stuxnet_dossier.pdf
Stuxnet enumerates the directories of a network resource. https://www.wired.com/images_blogs/threatlevel/2010/11/w32_stuxnet_dossier.pdf
Stuxnet uses encrypted configuration blocks and writes encrypted files to disk. https://www.wired.com/images_blogs/threatlevel/2010/11/w32_stuxnet_dossier.pdf
Stuxnet enumerates removable drives for infection. https://www.wired.com/images_blogs/threatlevel/2010/11/w32_stuxnet_dossier.pdf
Stuxnet injects an entire DLL into an existing, newly created, or preselected trusted process. https://www.wired.com/images_blogs/threatlevel/2010/11/w32_stuxnet_dossier.pdf
Stuxnet installs an RPC server for P2P communications. https://www.wired.com/images_blogs/threatlevel/2010/11/w32_stuxnet_dossier.pdf
Stuxnet searches the Registry for indicators of security programs. https://www.wired.com/images_blogs/threatlevel/2010/11/w32_stuxnet_dossier.pdf
Stuxnet can propagate via peer-to-peer communication and updates using RPC. https://www.wired.com/images_blogs/threatlevel/2010/11/w32_stuxnet_dossier.pdf
Stuxnet propagates to available network shares. https://www.wired.com/images_blogs/threatlevel/2010/11/w32_stuxnet_dossier.pdf
Stuxnet can propagate via removable media using an autorun.inf file or the CVE-2010-2568 LNK vulnerability. https://www.wired.com/images_blogs/threatlevel/2010/11/w32_stuxnet_dossier.pdf
Stuxnet uses a Windows rootkit to mask its binaries and other relevant files. https://www.wired.com/images_blogs/threatlevel/2010/11/w32_stuxnet_dossier.pdf
Stuxnet schedules a network job to execute two minutes after host infection. https://www.wired.com/images_blogs/threatlevel/2010/11/w32_stuxnet_dossier.pdf
Stuxnet used xp_cmdshell to store and execute SQL code. https://www.wired.com/images_blogs/threatlevel/2010/11/w32_stuxnet_dossier.pdf
Stuxnet calls LoadLibrary then executes exports from a DLL. https://www.wired.com/images_blogs/threatlevel/2010/11/w32_stuxnet_dossier.pdf
Stuxnet enumerates the currently running processes related to a variety of security products. https://www.wired.com/images_blogs/threatlevel/2010/11/w32_stuxnet_dossier.pdf
Stuxnet used a digitally signed driver with a compromised Realtek certificate. https://www.wired.com/images_blogs/threatlevel/2010/11/w32_stuxnet_dossier.pdf
Stuxnet collects system information including computer and domain names, OS version, and S7P paths. https://www.wired.com/images_blogs/threatlevel/2010/11/w32_stuxnet_dossier.pdf
Stuxnet collects the IP address of a compromised system. https://www.wired.com/images_blogs/threatlevel/2010/11/w32_stuxnet_dossier.pdf
Stuxnet collects the time and date of a system when it is infected. https://www.wired.com/images_blogs/threatlevel/2010/11/w32_stuxnet_dossier.pdf
Stuxnet infects remote servers via network shares and by infecting WinCC database views with malicious code. https://www.wired.com/images_blogs/threatlevel/2010/11/w32_stuxnet_dossier.pdf
Stuxnet infected WinCC machines via a hardcoded database server password. https://www.wired.com/images_blogs/threatlevel/2010/11/w32_stuxnet_dossier.pdf
Stuxnet attempts to access network resources with a domain account’s credentials. https://www.wired.com/images_blogs/threatlevel/2010/11/w32_stuxnet_dossier.pdf
Stuxnet used WMI with an explorer.exe token to execute on a remote share. https://www.wired.com/images_blogs/threatlevel/2010/11/w32_stuxnet_dossier.pdf

Stuxnet will store and execute SQL code that will extract and execute Stuxnet from the saved CAB file using xp_cmdshell with the following command: set @s = master..xp _ cmdshell extrac32 /y +@t+ +@t+x; exec(@s);  https://www.wired.com/images_blogs/threatlevel/2011/02/Symantec-Stuxnet-Update-Feb-2011.pdf

Stuxnet attempts to contact command and control servers on port 80 to send basic information about the computer it has compromised.  https://www.wired.com/images_blogs/threatlevel/2011/02/Symantec-Stuxnet-Update-Feb-2011.pdf

Stuxnet executes malicious SQL commands in the WinCC database server to propagate to remote systems. The malicious SQL commands include xp_cmdshell, sp_dumpdbilog, and sp_addextendedproc.  https://www.wired.com/images_blogs/threatlevel/2011/02/Symantec-Stuxnet-Update-Feb-2011.pdf

Stuxnet uses a hardcoded password in the WinCC software's database server as one of the mechanisms used to propagate to nearby systems.  https://www.wired.com/images_blogs/threatlevel/2011/02/Symantec-Stuxnet-Update-Feb-2011.pdf
Stuxnet modifies the Import Address Tables DLLs to hook specific APIs that are used to open project files.  https://www.wired.com/images_blogs/threatlevel/2011/02/Symantec-Stuxnet-Update-Feb-2011.pdf

Stuxnet copies the input area of an I/O image into data blocks with a one second interval between copies, forming a 21 second recording of the input area. The input area contains information being passed to the PLC from a peripheral. For example, the current state of a valve or the temperature of a device.  https://www.wired.com/images_blogs/threatlevel/2011/02/Symantec-Stuxnet-Update-Feb-2011.pdf

Stuxnet sends an SQL statement that creates a table and inserts a binary value into the table. The binary value is a hex string representation of the main Stuxnet DLL as an executable file (formed using resource 210) and an updated configuration data block.  https://www.wired.com/images_blogs/threatlevel/2011/02/Symantec-Stuxnet-Update-Feb-2011.pdf

When the peripheral output is written to, sequence C intercepts the output and ensures it is not written to the process image output. The output is the instructions the PLC sends to a device to change its operating behavior. By intercepting the peripheral output, Stuxnet prevents an operator from noticing unauthorized commands sent to the peripheral.  https://www.wired.com/images_blogs/threatlevel/2011/02/Symantec-Stuxnet-Update-Feb-2011.pdf

Stuxnet can reprogram a PLC and change critical parameters in such a way that legitimate commands can be overridden or intercepted. In addition, Stuxnet can apply inappropriate command sequences or parameters to cause damage to property.  https://www.wired.com/images_blogs/threatlevel/2011/02/Symantec-Stuxnet-Update-Feb-2011.pdf

Stuxnet manipulates the view of operators replaying process input and manipulating the I/O image to evade detection and inhibit protection functions.    https://www.langner.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/03/to-kill-a-centrifuge.pdf

Stuxnet renames s7otbxdx.dll, a dll responsible for handling communications with a PLC. It replaces this dll file with its own version that allows it to intercept any calls that are made to access the PLC.  https://www.wired.com/images_blogs/threatlevel/2011/02/Symantec-Stuxnet-Update-Feb-2011.pdf

Stuxnet infects OB1 so that its malicious code sequence is executed at the start of a cycle. It also infects OB35. OB35 acts as a watchdog, and on certain conditions, it can stop the execution of OB1.  https://www.wired.com/images_blogs/threatlevel/2011/02/Symantec-Stuxnet-Update-Feb-2011.pdf

In states 3 and 4 Stuxnet sends two network bursts (done through the DP_SEND primitive). The data in the frames are instructions for the frequency converter drives. For example one of the frames contains records that change the maximum frequency (the speed at which the motor will operate). The frequency converter drives consist of parameters, which can be remotely configured via Profibus. One can write new values to these parameters changing the behavior of the device.  https://www.wired.com/images_blogs/threatlevel/2011/02/Symantec-Stuxnet-Update-Feb-2011.pdf

Stuxnet infects PLCs with different code depending on the characteristics of the target system. An infection sequence consists of code blocks and data blocks that will be downloaded to the PLC to alter its behavior.  https://www.wired.com/images_blogs/threatlevel/2011/02/Symantec-Stuxnet-Update-Feb-2011.pdf

Stuxnet examines fields recorded by the DP_RECV monitor to determine if the target system is in a particular state of operation.  https://www.wired.com/images_blogs/threatlevel/2011/02/Symantec-Stuxnet-Update-Feb-2011.pdf

Stuxnet calls system function blocks which are part of the operating system running on the PLC. Theyre used to execute system tasks, such as reading the system clock (SFC1) and generating data blocks on the fly.  https://www.wired.com/images_blogs/threatlevel/2011/02/Symantec-Stuxnet-Update-Feb-2011.pdf

DP_RECV is the name of a standard function block used by network coprocessors. It is used to receive network frames on the Profibus a standard industrial network bus used for distributed I/O. The original block is copied to FC1869, and then replaced by a malicious block. Each time the function is used to receive a packet, the malicious Stuxnet block takes control: it will call the original DP_RECV in FC1869 and then perform postprocessing on the packet data. The replaced DP_RECV block (later on referred to as the DP_RECV monitor) is meant to monitor data sent by the frequency converter drives to the 315-2 CPU via CP 342-5 Profibus communication modules.  https://www.wired.com/images_blogs/threatlevel/2011/02/Symantec-Stuxnet-Update-Feb-2011.pdf

Stuxnet's infection sequence consists of code blocks and data blocks that will be downloaded to the PLC to alter its behavior.  https://www.wired.com/images_blogs/threatlevel/2011/02/Symantec-Stuxnet-Update-Feb-2011.pdf

Stuxnet copies itself into Step 7 projects in such a way that it automatically executes when the Step 7 project is loaded.  https://www.wired.com/images_blogs/threatlevel/2011/02/Symantec-Stuxnet-Update-Feb-2011.pdf

Stuxnet executes malicious SQL commands in the WinCC database server to propagate to remote systems. The malicious SQL commands include xp_cmdshell, sp_dumpdbilog, and sp_addextendedproc.  https://www.wired.com/images_blogs/threatlevel/2011/02/Symantec-Stuxnet-Update-Feb-2011.pdf

Stuxnet enumerates and parses the System Data Blocks (SDB) using the s7blk_findfirst and s7blk_findnext API calls in s7otbxdx.dll. Stuxnet must find an SDB with the DWORD at offset 50h equal to 0100CB2Ch. This specifies that the system uses the Profibus communications processor module CP 342-5. In addition, specific values are searched for and counted: 7050h and 9500h. 7050h is assigned to part number KFC750V3 which appears to be a frequency converter drive (also known as variable frequency drive) manufactured by Fararo Paya in Teheran, Iran. 9500h is assigned to Vacon NX frequency converter drives manufactured by Vacon based in Finland. 
Stuxnet was specifically targeting CPUs 6ES7-315-2 (Series 300) with special system data block characteristics for sequence A or B and 6ES7-315-2 for sequence C. The PLC type can also be checked using the s7ag_read_szl API. https://www.wired.com/images_blogs/threatlevel/2011/02/Symantec-Stuxnet-Update-Feb-2011.pdf

Stuxnet was able to self-replicate by being spread through removable drives. A willing insider or unknown third party, such as a contractor, may have brought the removable media into the target environment.   The earliest version of Stuxnet relied on physical installation, infecting target systems when an infected configuration file carried by a USB stick was opened.  https://www.wired.com/images_blogs/threatlevel/2011/02/Symantec-Stuxnet-Update-Feb-2011.pdf

One of Stuxnet's rootkits is contained entirely in the fake s7otbxdx.dll. In order to continue existing undetected on the PLC it needs to account for at least the following situations: read requests for its own malicious code blocks, read requests for infected blocks (OB1, OB35, DP_RECV), and write requests that could overwrite Stuxnets own code. Stuxnet contains code to monitor and intercept these types of requests. The rootkit modifies these requests so that Stuxnets PLC code is not discovered or damaged.  https://www.langner.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/03/to-kill-a-centrifuge.pdf

Stuxnet uses a thread to monitor a data block DB890 of sequence A or B. This thread is constantly running and probing this block (every 5 minutes). On an infected PLC, if block DB890 is found and contains a special magic value (used by Stuxnet to identify his own block DB890), this blocks data can be read and written. This thread is likely used to optimize the way sequences A and B work, and modify their behavior when the Step7 editor is opened.  https://www.wired.com/images_blogs/threatlevel/2011/02/Symantec-Stuxnet-Update-Feb-2011.pdf

Stuxnet infects DLL's associated with the WinCC Simatic manager which are responsible for opening project files. If a user opens an uninfected project file using a compromised manager, the file will be infected with Stuxnet code. If an infected project is opened with the Simatic manager, the modified data file will trigger a search for the xyz.dll file. If the xyz.dll file is not found in any of the specified locations, the malicious DLL will be loaded and executed by the manager.  https://www.wired.com/images_blogs/threatlevel/2011/02/Symantec-Stuxnet-Update-Feb-2011.pdf

SUNSPOT created a copy of the SolarWinds Orion software source file with a .bk extension to backup the original content, wrote SUNBURST using the same filename but with a .tmp extension, and then moved SUNBURST using MoveFileEx to the original filename with a .cs extension so it could be compiled within Orion software. https://www.crowdstrike.com/blog/sunspot-malware-technical-analysis/

SUNSPOT enumerated the Orion software Visual Studio solution directory path. https://www.crowdstrike.com/blog/sunspot-malware-technical-analysis/

Following the successful injection of SUNBURST, SUNSPOT deleted a temporary file it created named InventoryManager.bk after restoring the original SolarWinds Orion source code to the software library. https://www.crowdstrike.com/blog/sunspot-malware-technical-analysis/

SUNSPOT was identified on disk with a filename of taskhostsvc.exe and it created an encrypted log file at C:\Windows\Temp\vmware-vmdmp.log. https://www.crowdstrike.com/blog/sunspot-malware-technical-analysis/
SUNSPOT used Windows API functions such as MoveFileEx and NtQueryInformationProcess as part of the SUNBURST injection process. https://www.crowdstrike.com/blog/sunspot-malware-technical-analysis/

SUNSPOT encrypted log entries it collected with the stream cipher RC4 using a hard-coded key. It also uses AES128-CBC encrypted blobs for SUNBURST source code and data extracted from the SolarWinds Orion <MsBuild.exe process. https://www.crowdstrike.com/blog/sunspot-malware-technical-analysis/

SUNSPOT monitored running processes for instances of MsBuild.exe by hashing the name of each running process and comparing it to the corresponding value 0x53D525. It also extracted command-line arguments and individual arguments from the running MsBuild.exe process to identify the directory path of the Orion software Visual Studio solution. https://www.crowdstrike.com/blog/sunspot-malware-technical-analysis/
SUNSPOT malware was designed and used to insert SUNBURST into software builds of the SolarWinds Orion IT management product. https://www.crowdstrike.com/blog/sunspot-malware-technical-analysis/

Use: T9000 encrypts collected data using a single byte XOR key. http://researchcenter.paloaltonetworks.com/2016/02/t9000-advanced-modular-backdoor-uses-complex-anti-analysis-techniques/

T9000 uses the Skype API to record audio and video calls. It writes encrypted data to %APPDATA%\Intel\Skype. http://researchcenter.paloaltonetworks.com/2016/02/t9000-advanced-modular-backdoor-uses-complex-anti-analysis-techniques/

T9000 searches removable storage devices for files with a pre-defined list of file extensions (e.g. * .doc, .ppt, .xls, .docx, .pptx, *.xlsx). Any matching files are encrypted and written to a local user directory. http://researchcenter.paloaltonetworks.com/2016/02/t9000-advanced-modular-backdoor-uses-complex-anti-analysis-techniques/

If a victim meets certain criteria, T9000 uses the AppInit_DLL functionality to achieve persistence by ensuring that every user mode process that is spawned will load its malicious DLL, ResN32.dll. It does this by creating the following Registry keys: HKLM\Software\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Windows\AppInit_DLLs – %APPDATA%\Intel\ResN32.dll and HKLM\Software\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Windows\LoadAppInit_DLLs – 0x1. http://researchcenter.paloaltonetworks.com/2016/02/t9000-advanced-modular-backdoor-uses-complex-anti-analysis-techniques/

During the T9000 installation process, it drops a copy of the legitimate Microsoft binary igfxtray.exe. The executable contains a side-loading weakness which is used to load a portion of the malware. http://researchcenter.paloaltonetworks.com/2016/02/t9000-advanced-modular-backdoor-uses-complex-anti-analysis-techniques/
T9000 searches through connected drives for removable storage devices. http://researchcenter.paloaltonetworks.com/2016/02/t9000-advanced-modular-backdoor-uses-complex-anti-analysis-techniques/

T9000 can take screenshots of the desktop and target application windows, saving them to user directories as one byte XOR encrypted .dat files. http://researchcenter.paloaltonetworks.com/2016/02/t9000-advanced-modular-backdoor-uses-complex-anti-analysis-techniques/

T9000 performs checks for various antivirus and security products during installation. http://researchcenter.paloaltonetworks.com/2016/02/t9000-advanced-modular-backdoor-uses-complex-anti-analysis-techniques/

T9000 gathers and beacons the operating system build number and CPU Architecture (32-bit/64-bit) during installation. http://researchcenter.paloaltonetworks.com/2016/02/t9000-advanced-modular-backdoor-uses-complex-anti-analysis-techniques/
T9000 gathers and beacons the MAC and IP addresses during installation. http://researchcenter.paloaltonetworks.com/2016/02/t9000-advanced-modular-backdoor-uses-complex-anti-analysis-techniques/

T9000 gathers and beacons the username of the logged in account during installation. It will also gather the username of running processes to determine if it is running as SYSTEM. http://researchcenter.paloaltonetworks.com/2016/02/t9000-advanced-modular-backdoor-uses-complex-anti-analysis-techniques/
T9000 gathers and beacons the system time during installation. http://researchcenter.paloaltonetworks.com/2016/02/t9000-advanced-modular-backdoor-uses-complex-anti-analysis-techniques/

T9000 uses the Skype API to record audio and video calls. It writes encrypted data to %APPDATA%\Intel\Skype. http://researchcenter.paloaltonetworks.com/2016/02/t9000-advanced-modular-backdoor-uses-complex-anti-analysis-techniques/

Use: ThiefQuest uploads files via unencrypted HTTP.   https://objective-see.com/blog/blog_0x60.html
ThiefQuest uses AppleScript's osascript -e command to launch ThiefQuest's persistence via Launch Agent and Launch Daemon.  https://objective-see.com/blog/blog_0x59.html

ThiefQuest searches through the /Users/ folder looking for executable files. For each executable, ThiefQuest prepends a copy of itself to the beginning of the file. When the file is executed, the ThiefQuest code is executed first. ThiefQuest creates a hidden file, copies the original target executable to the file, then executes the new hidden file to maintain the appearance of normal behavior.   https://objective-see.com/blog/blog_0x60.html

ThiefQuest installs a launch item using an embedded encrypted launch agent property list template. The plist file is installed in the ~/Library/LaunchAgents/ folder and configured with the path to the persistent binary located in the ~/Library/ folder. https://objective-see.com/blog/blog_0x59.html

When running with root privileges after a Launch Agent is installed, ThiefQuest installs a plist file to the /Library/LaunchDaemons/ folder with the RunAtLoad key set to true establishing persistence as a Launch Daemon.  https://objective-see.com/blog/blog_0x59.html
ThiefQuest encrypts a set of file extensions on a host, deletes the original files, and provides a ransom note with no contact information. https://objective-see.com/blog/blog_0x60.html

ThiefQuest uses a function named is_debugging to perform anti-debugging logic. The function invokes sysctl checking the returned value of P_TRACED. ThiefQuest also calls ptrace with the PTRACE_DENY_ATTACH flag to prevent debugging. https://objective-see.com/blog/blog_0x60.html

ThiefQuest exfiltrates targeted file extensions in the /Users/ folder to the command and control server via unencrypted HTTP. Network packets contain a string with two pieces of information: a file path and the contents of the file in a base64 encoded string.  https://objective-see.com/blog/blog_0x60.html
ThiefQuest hides a copy of itself in the user's ~/Library directory by using a . at the beginning of the file name followed by 9 random characters. https://objective-see.com/blog/blog_0x59.html
ThiefQuest uses the function kill_unwanted to obtain a list of running processes and kills each process matching a list of security related processes. https://objective-see.com/blog/blog_0x59.html
ThiefQuest can download and execute payloads in-memory or from disk. https://objective-see.com/blog/blog_0x60.html
ThiefQuest uses the CGEventTap functions to perform keylogging. https://www.trendmicro.com/en_us/research/20/g/updates-on-quickly-evolving-thiefquest-macos-malware.html
ThiefQuest prepends a copy of itself to the beginning of an executable file while maintaining the name of the executable.  https://objective-see.com/blog/blog_0x60.html
ThiefQuest uses various API to perform behaviors such as executing payloads and performing local enumeration. https://objective-see.com/blog/blog_0x60.html
ThiefQuest obtains a list of running processes using the function kill_unwanted. https://objective-see.com/blog/blog_0x59.html
ThiefQuest uses various API functions such as NSCreateObjectFileImageFromMemory to load and link in-memory payloads. https://objective-see.com/blog/blog_0x60.html

ThiefQuest uses the kill_unwanted function to get a list of running processes, compares each process with an encrypted list of "unwanted" security related programs, and kills the processes for security related programs. https://objective-see.com/blog/blog_0x59.html

ThiefQuest invokes time call to check the system's time, executes a sleep command, invokes a second time call, and then compares the time difference between the two time calls and the amount of time the system slept to identify the sandbox. https://objective-see.com/blog/blog_0x59.html

Use: Triada encrypts data prior to exfiltration. https://security.googleblog.com/2019/06/pha-family-highlights-triada.html

TrickBot can send information about the compromised host and upload data to a hardcoded C2 server.  https://www.cybereason.com/blog/dropping-anchor-from-a-trickbot-infection-to-the-discovery-of-the-anchor-malware

TrickBot utilizes EternalBlue and EternalRomance exploits for lateral movement in the modules wormwinDll, wormDll, mwormDll, nwormDll, tabDll. https://www.welivesecurity.com/2020/10/12/eset-takes-part-global-operation-disrupt-trickbot/

TrickBot can use secondary C2 servers for communication after establishing connectivity and relaying victim information to primary C2 servers. https://www.cybereason.com/blog/dropping-anchor-from-a-trickbot-infection-to-the-discovery-of-the-anchor-malware

TrickBot searches the system for all of the following file extensions: .avi, .mov, .mkv, .mpeg, .mpeg4, .mp4, .mp3, .wav, .ogg, .jpeg, .jpg, .png, .bmp, .gif, .tiff, .ico, .xlsx, and .zip. It can also obtain browsing history, cookies, and plug-in information.  https://www.securityartwork.es/wp-content/uploads/2017/07/Trickbot-report-S2-Grupo.pdf
TrickBot module "Trickboot" can write or erase the UEFI/BIOS firmware of a compromised device. https://eclypsium.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/12/TrickBot-Now-Offers-TrickBoot-Persist-Brick-Profit.pdf
TrickBot can disable Windows Defender. https://blog.trendmicro.com/trendlabs-security-intelligence/trickbot-shows-off-new-trick-password-grabber-module/
TrickBot downloads several additional files and saves them to the victim's machine.  https://www.trendmicro.com/vinfo/us/threat-encyclopedia/malware/tspy_trickload.n

TrickBot has the ability to capture RDP credentials by capturing the CredEnumerateA API https://blog.trendmicro.com/trendlabs-security-intelligence/trickbot-adds-remote-application-credential-grabbing-capabilities-to-its-repertoire/
TrickBot used COM to setup scheduled task for persistence. https://www.welivesecurity.com/2020/10/12/eset-takes-part-global-operation-disrupt-trickbot/
The TrickBot downloader has used an icon to appear as a Microsoft Word document. https://www.cybereason.com/blog/dropping-anchor-from-a-trickbot-infection-to-the-discovery-of-the-anchor-malware
TrickBot can modify registry entries. https://blog.trendmicro.com/trendlabs-security-intelligence/trickbot-shows-off-new-trick-password-grabber-module/

TrickBot uses the Windows API call, CreateProcessW(), to manage execution flow.  TrickBot has also used Nt* API functions to perform Process Injection. https://www.securityartwork.es/wp-content/uploads/2017/07/Trickbot-report-S2-Grupo.pdf
TrickBot module shareDll/mshareDll discovers network shares via the WNetOpenEnumA API.  https://www.welivesecurity.com/2020/10/12/eset-takes-part-global-operation-disrupt-trickbot/

Some TrickBot samples have used HTTP over ports 447 and 8082 for C2.    Newer versions of TrickBot have been known to use a custom communication protocol which sends the data unencrypted over port 443.  https://www.securityartwork.es/wp-content/uploads/2017/07/Trickbot-report-S2-Grupo.pdf

TrickBot uses non-descriptive names to hide functionality and uses an AES CBC (256 bits) encryption algorithm for its loader and configuration files. https://www.securityartwork.es/wp-content/uploads/2017/07/Trickbot-report-S2-Grupo.pdf
TrickBot leverages a custom packer to obfuscate its functionality. https://www.securityartwork.es/wp-content/uploads/2017/07/Trickbot-report-S2-Grupo.pdf
TrickBot can identify the groups the user on a compromised host belongs to. https://www.cybereason.com/blog/dropping-anchor-from-a-trickbot-infection-to-the-discovery-of-the-anchor-malware

TrickBot has used an email with an Excel sheet containing a malicious macro to deploy the malware https://blog.trendmicro.com/trendlabs-security-intelligence/trickbot-adds-remote-application-credential-grabbing-capabilities-to-its-repertoire/
TrickBot has been delivered via malicious links in phishing e-mails. https://www.cybereason.com/blog/dropping-anchor-from-a-trickbot-infection-to-the-discovery-of-the-anchor-malware
TrickBot can implant malicious code into a compromised device's firmware. https://eclypsium.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/12/TrickBot-Now-Offers-TrickBoot-Persist-Brick-Profit.pdf
TrickBot uses module networkDll for process list discovery.  https://www.welivesecurity.com/2020/10/12/eset-takes-part-global-operation-disrupt-trickbot/
TrickBot has used Nt* Native API functions to inject code into legitimate processes such as wermgr.exe. https://www.joesecurity.org/blog/498839998833561473
TrickBot injects into the svchost.exe process.    https://www.securityartwork.es/wp-content/uploads/2017/07/Trickbot-report-S2-Grupo.pdf
TrickBot has been known to reach a command and control server via one of nine proxy IP addresses.    https://www.bitdefender.com/blog/labs/trickbot-is-dead-long-live-trickbot/
TrickBot uses vncDll module to remote control the victim machine.  https://www.welivesecurity.com/2020/10/12/eset-takes-part-global-operation-disrupt-trickbot/

TrickBot has used a VNC module to monitor the victim and collect information to pivot to valuable systems on the network   https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/trickbot-updates-its-vnc-module-for-high-value-targets/
TrickBot can enumerate computers and network devices. https://www.cybereason.com/blog/dropping-anchor-from-a-trickbot-infection-to-the-discovery-of-the-anchor-malware
TrickBot creates a scheduled task on the system that provides persistence.   https://www.securityartwork.es/wp-content/uploads/2017/07/Trickbot-report-S2-Grupo.pdf
TrickBot has come with a signed downloader component. https://www.cybereason.com/blog/dropping-anchor-from-a-trickbot-infection-to-the-discovery-of-the-anchor-malware

TrickBot gathers the OS version, machine name, CPU type, amount of RAM available, and UEFI/BIOS firmware information from the victim’s machine.    https://www.securityartwork.es/wp-content/uploads/2017/07/Trickbot-report-S2-Grupo.pdf
TrickBot obtains the IP address, location, and other relevant network information from the victim’s machine.   https://www.securityartwork.es/wp-content/uploads/2017/07/Trickbot-report-S2-Grupo.pdf
TrickBot can identify the user and groups the user belongs to on a compromised host. https://www.cybereason.com/blog/dropping-anchor-from-a-trickbot-infection-to-the-discovery-of-the-anchor-malware
TrickBot collects a list of install programs and services on the system’s machine. https://www.securityartwork.es/wp-content/uploads/2017/07/Trickbot-report-S2-Grupo.pdf

TrickBot can obtain passwords stored in files from several applications such as Outlook, Filezilla, OpenSSH, OpenVPN and WinSCP.   Additionally, it searches for the ".vnc.lnk" affix to steal VNC credentials. https://blog.trendmicro.com/trendlabs-security-intelligence/trickbot-shows-off-new-trick-password-grabber-module/

TrickBot has retrieved PuTTY credentials by querying the Software\SimonTatham\Putty\Sessions registry key  https://blog.trendmicro.com/trendlabs-security-intelligence/trickbot-adds-remote-application-credential-grabbing-capabilities-to-its-repertoire/

TrickBot has attempted to get users to launch malicious documents to deliver its payload.   https://blog.trendmicro.com/trendlabs-security-intelligence/trickbot-adds-remote-application-credential-grabbing-capabilities-to-its-repertoire/
TrickBot has used printf and file I/O loops to delay process execution as part of API hammering. https://www.joesecurity.org/blog/498839998833561473
